title: Building the Cerebral Cortex
summary: How stem cells generate, position and wire the neurons of the six-layered cortex.

lessons.title: Radial Glia and Outer Radial Glia as Neural Stem Cells

levels.kid:
Your brain's thinking layer, the **cortex**, was built before you were born. Who built it? Special helper cells called **radial glia**.

A radial glia cell is long and thin, like a rope stretched from the bottom of the growing brain to the top. It does two jobs. First, it splits to make new brain cells. Second, its long rope is a climbing path that baby neurons crawl along to reach their homes.

People have an extra kind called **outer radial glia**. They sit higher up and keep making even more neurons. That is one reason the human brain grew so big and wrinkly.

So radial glia are both the factory and the road!
levels.hs:
The **cerebral cortex** is the brain's folded outer layer. Its billions of neurons come from **neural stem cells**: cells that can copy themselves and also make specialized cells.

Early on, the developing brain wall is a thin sheet of **neuroepithelial cells** lining the fluid-filled ventricles. Around the time neurons start being made, these cells turn into **radial glia**. Each radial glial cell has its body near the ventricle, in a zone called the **ventricular zone (VZ)**, and a long fiber that reaches all the way to the brain's outer surface.

Radial glia divide in two main ways:
- **Symmetric division**: one cell makes two radial glia, which grows the stem cell pool.
- **Asymmetric division**: one cell makes one radial glia plus a neuron or an **intermediate progenitor**, a cell that divides a few more times before becoming neurons.

Their long fibers also act as scaffolds that newborn neurons follow outward.

In humans and other primates, a thick extra layer called the **outer subventricular zone (OSVZ)** holds **outer radial glia (oRG)**. These cells have lost their connection to the ventricle but keep the fiber to the surface. They divide many times, which adds a huge number of neurons. Scientists think oRG help explain why the human cortex is so large and folded.
levels.college:
Cortical neurogenesis follows a lineage from **neuroepithelial cells** to **apical radial glia (aRG)**, then to **intermediate progenitors (IPs)**, and finally to neurons.

**Apical radial glia** are bipolar cells:
- An apical endfoot at the ventricle, with adherens junctions and a primary cilium facing the cerebrospinal fluid.
- A basal process anchored to the pial basement membrane.
- Markers include **PAX6**, **SOX2**, **Nestin**, **GLAST** and **BLBP (FABP7)**.

They show **interkinetic nuclear migration (INM)**: the nucleus moves basally during G1, enters S phase away from the ventricle, then returns apically so mitosis happens at the ventricular surface.

Division modes shift over time. Early divisions are mostly **proliferative** and symmetric. Later divisions become mostly **neurogenic** and asymmetric. **Notch signaling** keeps progenitors in the stem state: daughters that receive more Notch activity, through targets such as **HES1** and **HES5**, stay progenitors. Daughters that express proneural genes and Delta ligands differentiate.

**Intermediate progenitors** (TBR2/EOMES+) move into the **subventricular zone (SVZ)**. They lack radial fibers and usually divide once or a few times to make neurons. This amplifies the output of each radial glial cell.

**Outer radial glia (basal RG)** are found in the OSVZ:
- They have a basal fiber but no apical attachment.
- They express PAX6, **HOPX**, **PTPRZ1**, **TNC** and **FAM107A**.
- They undergo **mitotic somal translocation**: the cell body jumps basally just before dividing.
- They self-renew repeatedly and generate many IPs.

The OSVZ is enormously expanded in primates. Rodents have few oRG and a smooth (lissencephalic) cortex, while ferrets and primates have many oRG and folded (gyrencephalic) cortices. Late in development, radial glia switch to making astrocytes and oligodendrocyte lineages. Some become ependymal cells or adult neural stem cells.
levels.phd:
Radial glia were long viewed purely as migration scaffolds, described by Rakic in the 1970s. Their stem cell identity was established in 2001 by Noctor, Kriegstein and colleagues, and by Miyata and colleagues. Using retroviral labeling and time-lapse imaging in slices, they showed that radial glia divide asymmetrically to self-renew and produce neurons, and that their clonal progeny migrate along the parent fiber. Noctor et al. (2004) then showed that neurogenesis proceeds in two steps through Tbr2+ intermediate progenitors in the SVZ.

**Fate determinants.** Asymmetric fate tracks with the inheritance of cellular components:
- The apical membrane and junctional complex (Par3/Par6/aPKC).
- The basal process.
- Older versus younger centrosomes (Wang et al., 2009, in mouse).
- Factors such as Numb/Numbl that antagonize Notch.

Cleavage-plane orientation is governed by the spindle machinery (LGN/NuMA, Insc), but it predicts fate only loosely. The loss of apical contact is a key signal for leaving the stem state.

**Cell-cycle length hypothesis.** Lengthening of G1 correlates with neurogenic division. In Calegari and Huttner's experiments, shortening G1 by overexpressing Cdk4/cyclinD1 expanded the progenitor pool, while lengthening it promoted neurogenesis.

**oRG discovery.** Hansen et al. (2010) and Fietz et al. (2010) characterized human oRG. Pollen et al. (2015) used single-cell RNA sequencing to define the oRG signature (HOPX, PTPRZ1, TNC, LIFR, FAM107A). Their maintenance depends on cell-intrinsic programs and on niche signals, including LIFR/STAT3, PDGFD-PDGFRβ, and integrin interactions with ECM components that oRG secrete themselves.

**Human-specific genes.** **ARHGAP11B**, which arose by partial duplication of ARHGAP11A, increases basal progenitors and can induce folding when expressed in mouse or ferret (Florio et al., 2015). **NOTCH2NL** paralogs, located at 1q21.1, delay differentiation by enhancing Notch signaling (Fiddes; Suzuki, 2018). **TBC1D3** also expands oRG.

**Discontinuous scaffold.** In primates, the radial scaffold becomes discontinuous at mid-gestation (Nowakowski et al., 2016). Truncated aRG fibers end in the OSVZ, and later neurons climb oRG fibers instead.
levels.expert:
Progenitor biology underlies several neurodevelopmental disorders, and it frames how we interpret them.

**Microcephaly as a progenitor disease.** Primary microcephaly (MCPH) genes are enriched for centrosomal and spindle proteins. Examples are **ASPM**, **WDR62**, **CDK5RAP2**, **CENPJ** and **MCPH1**. Defects tend to cause premature neurogenic divisions or progenitor apoptosis, which depletes the founder pool. This is why mouse models often show disproportionately mild phenotypes, while ASPM loss in ferrets, a species with abundant oRG, reproduces substantial cortical shrinkage (Johnson et al., 2018). The species chosen for a model matters.

**Zika virus.** ZIKV preferentially infects radial glia, including oRG, partly via the receptor candidate **AXL**, which is highly expressed by these cells. AXL knockout did not prevent infection in organoids, however, so entry is likely multi-receptor. Infection causes progenitor death and cell-cycle disruption, which explains congenital microcephaly. Cerebral organoids were central to establishing this causal link.

**Malformations of cortical development.** Somatic mTOR-pathway variants (MTOR, PIK3CA, DEPDC5) arising in a radial glial cell propagate to its clonal neuronal progeny. This produces focal cortical dysplasia and hemimegalencephaly, a key target in epilepsy surgery. The proportion of cells carrying the variant (variant allele fraction) can be very low, so deep sequencing of resected tissue is often needed. Bulk blood testing misses these variants.

**Organoid pitfalls.** Organoids recapitulate aRG and oRG but under-form a true OSVZ. They also show cellular stress signatures (ER stress, glycolysis) that impair subtype specification (Bhaduri et al., 2020). Transplantation into rodent cortex, and newer protocols, partly rescue maturation.

**Open questions.**
- Is oRG abundance a cause of folding, or one contributor alongside mechanical buckling and regional proliferation gradients? Folding can arise without dramatic oRG expansion in some species.
- How do outer radial glia (oRG) give rise to gliomas? Glioblastoma cells reactivate an oRG-like program (HOPX, PTPRZ1, and somal translocation behavior), which may underlie invasion.
- How do lineage-tracing technologies such as barcoding (for example, somatic mutation lineage reconstruction in human postmortem brain) refine clonal output estimates?

keyPoints: Radial glia are the main neural stem cells of the developing cortex
Their long basal fiber also serves as a migration scaffold
Divisions shift from symmetric proliferative to asymmetric neurogenic
Intermediate progenitors (TBR2+) amplify neuron output in the SVZ
Outer radial glia (HOPX+) in the OSVZ drive primate cortical expansion
Progenitor defects cause microcephaly; ZIKV targets radial glia

test.q: Where are the cell bodies of apical radial glia located?
test.explain: Apical radial glia sit in the ventricular zone with an endfoot touching the ventricle. Outer radial glia sit in the OSVZ instead.

test.q: A radial glial cell divides into one radial glial cell and one neuron. This is a:
test.explain: One daughter self-renews and the other differentiates, so the division is asymmetric and neurogenic.

test.q: Which feature distinguishes outer radial glia from apical radial glia?
choices: They lack a basal radial fiber
test.explain: Outer radial glia keep a basal fiber, express PAX6 and self-renew repeatedly, but have lost contact with the ventricle.

test.q: Which transcription factor marks intermediate progenitors?
test.explain: TBR2/EOMES marks intermediate progenitors in the SVZ. HOPX marks outer radial glia, and SOX2 and GLAST mark radial glial cells.

test.q: Higher Notch signaling in a daughter cell tends to:
test.explain: Notch targets such as HES1 and HES5 maintain the stem state.

test.q: The movement of the radial glial nucleus during the cell cycle, with mitosis at the ventricle, is called:
test.explain: In interkinetic nuclear migration, the nucleus moves basally in G1/S and apically for mitosis. Mitotic somal translocation is a behavior of outer radial glia.

test.q: Why is the OSVZ linked to human cortical size?
choices: It holds abundant self-renewing outer radial glia
It produces most of the brain's spinal fluid
It is the site of synaptic pruning in infancy
test.explain: Outer radial glia divide repeatedly in the expanded OSVZ, adding many neurons.

test.q: Besides making neurons, radial glia fibers serve as:
test.explain: Newborn neurons climb along radial glial fibers to reach the cortical plate.

test.q: Late in development, radial glia mainly switch to producing:
test.explain: Radial glia make astrocytes and oligodendrocyte lineages later on. Microglia come from yolk-sac precursors, not radial glia.

test.q: Outer radial glia show mitotic somal ___, a basal jump of the cell body just before division.
test.explain: Mitotic somal translocation is a hallmark behavior of outer radial glia.

test.q: What are the cells called that radial glia arise from in the early brain wall?
test.explain: Neuroepithelial cells transform into radial glia around the onset of neurogenesis.

test.q: Lab studies of human outer radial glia identified ___ as a key marker gene.
test.explain: HOPX is a widely used oRG marker, along with PTPRZ1 and TNC.

kidTest.q: What do radial glia make?
kidTest.explain: Radial glia split to make new brain cells.

kidTest.q: What is a radial glia cell shaped like?
kidTest.explain: It is long and thin, stretching across the growing brain.

kidTest.q: What do baby neurons use the long fiber for?
choices: To grab food while they grow
To send messages to other cells
kidTest.explain: The fiber is like a road that baby neurons crawl along to reach their home.

kidTest.q: Which extra helper cells help make the human brain big?
kidTest.explain: Outer radial glia keep making many more neurons.

kidTest.q: The brain's thinking layer is the c _ _ _ _ x.
kidTest.explain: The cortex is built by radial glia before birth.

advancedTest.q: ASPM loss causes mild cortical shrinkage in mice but marked shrinkage in ferrets. The best explanation is:
choices: Mouse ASPM is a pseudogene with no function
Ferrets largely lack intermediate progenitors in the SVZ
Ferret cortex relies more on oRG-driven expansion
Ferret neurons migrate tangentially instead of radially
advancedTest.explain: Gyrencephalic ferrets rely on abundant outer radial glia, so progenitor defects show more strongly in them than in lissencephalic mice.

advancedTest.q: Shortening G1 by overexpressing Cdk4/cyclinD1 in progenitors would be predicted to:
advancedTest.explain: According to the cell-cycle length hypothesis, a longer G1 favors neurogenesis. A shorter G1 therefore favors proliferative divisions.

advancedTest.q: A child with focal cortical dysplasia has a normal blood gene panel. The best next step on resected tissue is:
choices: Test serum for Zika virus antibodies in the child
Repeat the blood karyotype at higher resolution
Deep sequencing for somatic mTOR variants
advancedTest.explain: The variant arises in one radial glial clone at low variant allele fraction, so it is absent from blood and needs deep tissue sequencing.

advancedTest.q: Why don't organoid findings alone settle whether oRG cause cortical folding?
choices: Folding has many causes and organoids lack a true OSVZ
Organoids mostly form spinal cord tissue rather than cortex
oRG markers are absent from fetal human tissue
Organoids contain too few radial glia to study
advancedTest.explain: Folding involves mechanics and proliferation gradients as well as oRG, and organoids under-form the OSVZ and show stress signatures.

lessons.title: Inside-Out Layering and Neurogenesis Timing

levels.kid:
Your brain's wrinkly outer layer, the **cortex**, is built like a layered cake with six layers. But it is built in a funny order.

The first brain cells to be made stay deep down, close to the middle. Every new batch of cells climbs up past the older ones and settles on top. So the newest cells end up near the outside. Scientists call this **inside-out** building.

Imagine kids lining up for a photo. The first kids sit in the front row near the floor. Each new group has to step past them to stand higher up.

Timing matters too. Cells made early become deep-layer cells. Cells made later become top-layer cells. If the timing or order goes wrong, the brain may not work properly.
levels.hs:
The **cerebral cortex** in mammals has **six layers**, numbered I (at the surface) to VI (deepest). Each layer holds different kinds of neurons with different jobs. For example, layer V neurons send long axons down to the spinal cord, while layers II/III neurons mostly connect one part of the cortex to another.

These neurons are born from stem cells lining the fluid-filled ventricles deep inside the developing brain. The process of making new neurons is called **neurogenesis**. In humans it happens mostly between about weeks 6 and 20 of pregnancy, roughly the first half.

The layers form **inside-out**:
- The earliest-born neurons settle in the deepest layers (VI, then V).
- Later-born neurons migrate *past* them to form layers IV, then III and II.
- Layer I is the exception. It is made mostly of very early cells called **Cajal-Retzius cells**.

This means a neuron's **birthdate** largely predicts which layer it will live in.

Scientists discovered this in the 1960s using a chemical tag called tritiated thymidine. It labels cells that are copying their DNA on the day it is given. Labeling early marked deep neurons, and labeling late marked upper ones.

When this layering fails, as in the genetic disorder **lissencephaly** ("smooth brain"), children can have severe seizures and intellectual disability.
levels.college:
**Cortical neurogenesis** produces the excitatory projection neurons of the neocortex from progenitors in the ventricular and subventricular zones. These neurons are generated in a stereotyped temporal order that maps onto laminar position.

**Sequence of events**
- The first postmitotic neurons form the **preplate**. It contains Cajal-Retzius cells and subplate neurons.
- The first cortical plate neurons **split the preplate** into a superficial **marginal zone** (future layer I) and a deep **subplate**.
- Each successive cohort passes through the subplate and existing cortical plate, then stops beneath the marginal zone. The result is the order VI → V → IV → II/III.

The pattern was established by **Angevine and Sidman (1961)** using [3H]-thymidine birthdating in mice, and later confirmed in primates by **Rakic (1974)**. In mice, neurogenesis runs from about embryonic day 11 to 17. In humans it runs from about gestational week 6 to the second trimester.

**Molecular identity by layer** (with markers):
- Subplate/layer VI corticothalamic neurons: **TBR1**, FOXP2
- Layer V subcerebral neurons: **CTIP2 (BCL11B)**, FEZF2
- Layers II–IV callosal and intracortical neurons: **SATB2**, CUX1/CUX2, BRN2

These transcription factors repress one another. For example, SATB2 represses Ctip2, and FEZF2 promotes Ctip2. This mutual repression sharpens fate boundaries.

**Stopping position** depends on **Reelin**, secreted by Cajal-Retzius cells. Reelin binds VLDLR and ApoER2 receptors, which triggers phosphorylation of **DAB1**. In the *reeler* mouse, which lacks Reelin, the preplate fails to split and layering is roughly inverted (outside-in).

In humans, *RELN* and *VLDLR* mutations cause lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia. This shows that layer order is genetically controlled.
levels.phd:
A central question is how progenitor competence changes over time so that one lineage yields deep-layer and then upper-layer neurons.

**Heterochronic transplantation.** McConnell and Kaznowski (1991) transplanted ferret progenitors between ages. Early progenitors placed in older hosts switched to upper-layer fates if transplanted before their final S-phase. Late progenitors placed in young hosts did not revert to deep fates. This revealed a **progressive restriction of competence**. Later work (Desai and McConnell) showed that early progenitors' choices are cell-intrinsically biased.

**Intrinsic temporal programs.** Cultured mouse cortical progenitors and ES-cell-derived cortical cells (Shen et al. 2006; Gaspard et al. 2008) reproduce the deep-then-superficial sequence in vitro. So much of the program is intrinsic. Key regulators include:
- **FOXG1**: it represses early Cajal-Retzius fate. Conditional loss converts progenitors back to producing CR-like cells.
- **Ikaros**: it sustains early deep-layer competence.
- Feedback from postmitotic neurons: deep-layer neurons secrete signals such as neurotrophin-3 and FGF9 that push progenitors toward later fates.

**Common versus multiple lineages.** Clonal analyses conflict. Franco et al. (2012) proposed a **Cux2+ progenitor** fate-restricted to upper layers. Guo et al. (2013) and Gil-Sanz et al. (2015) found that individual radial glia generate both deep and upper neurons sequentially. Current consensus favors a largely common, temporally progressing progenitor. **Mosaic analysis with double markers** (Gao et al. 2014) showed that each radial glial unit makes roughly 8–9 excitatory neurons, distributed across layers.

**Single-cell transcriptomics.** Telley et al. (2019) used FlashTag to pulse-label birthdated cohorts. They found that apical progenitors shift from internally driven to more environment-responsive transcriptional states over time.

**Cell-cycle kinetics.** The G1 phase lengthens across neurogenesis (Takahashi, Nowakowski and Caviness), and the proportion of cells leaving the cycle (the Q fraction) rises. This shift in cycle timing is linked to neurogenic output.
levels.expert:
Several clinically relevant points follow from inside-out layering and timing.

**Primate expansion through prolonged neurogenesis.** Human neurogenesis lasts roughly ten times longer than in mice. During this window **outer subventricular zone** progenitors massively amplify the supragranular layers (II/III). These layers make up a far larger share of human cortex and carry corticocortical connections. Human-specific gene duplications, notably *NOTCH2NL* (Fiddes et al., Suzuki et al. 2018), delay differentiation. *ARHGAP11B* amplifies basal progenitors. Slower human-specific developmental tempo, reflected in differences in metabolic and proteostatic timing, also contributes. Cortical organoids reproduce the deep-then-upper order but compress and blur the sequence, so laminar conclusions from organoids need caution.

**Timing of insults predicts pathology.** Because birthdate determines layer, insults hitting a specific gestational window select for vulnerable cohorts:
- Congenital **Zika** virus and **cytomegalovirus** target progenitors. The earlier the infection, the more severe the microcephaly and cortical malformation.
- Fetal radiation and some teratogens cause greater harm during peak neurogenesis than later.
- Upper-layer deficits are thought to be over-represented in autism. Transcriptomic data (Velmeshev et al. 2019) implicate layer II/III excitatory neurons. Bulk transcriptomic co-expression data also map risk genes onto mid-fetal deep-layer neurons (Willsey et al. 2013, based on co-expression network analysis).

**Pitfalls in interpreting markers.** Layer markers are not absolute identity labels. CTIP2 is co-expressed in some callosal neurons, and SATB2 appears in subcerebral neurons in early development. Laminar position and molecular identity can uncouple. In *reeler* mice, neurons keep birthdate-appropriate molecular identities and projections despite misplacement. In children with neuronal ectopias, displaced neurons may still be wired, which contributes to epileptogenic networks.

**Open questions**
- How is an intrinsic clock implemented? Candidates include chromatin regulators such as Polycomb, which times the switch from neurogenesis to gliogenesis.
- Why do humans retain a late, protracted upper-layer phase?
- Can temporal fate be reprogrammed? Experimental restoration of competence in late progenitors (for example, by manipulating Polycomb or FOXG1) is possible. However, translating this into repair of malformations remains speculative.

keyPoints: The neocortex has six layers, with layer I at the surface and layer VI deepest
Layers form inside-out: early-born neurons go deep, later-born neurons migrate past them
Layer I comes from early Cajal-Retzius cells after the preplate splits
Birthdate predicts layer, shown by thymidine birthdating (Angevine & Sidman 1961)
Layer markers include TBR1 (VI), CTIP2 (V) and SATB2/CUX2 (upper layers)
Reelin controls where neurons stop; the reeler mouse shows roughly inverted layers

test.q: In the inside-out pattern, where do the earliest-born cortical plate neurons end up?
choices: In layer I at the surface
test.explain: Early-born neurons settle deep (VI, then V). Later cohorts migrate past them to more superficial layers.

test.q: Which cells make up most of layer I in the developing cortex?
test.explain: Layer I comes from the marginal zone, which contains early-born Cajal-Retzius cells.

test.q: What did Angevine and Sidman's 1961 thymidine experiments show?
choices: A neuron's birthdate predicts its layer
Radial glia are neural stem cells

test.q: The preplate splits into which two structures?
test.explain: The first cortical plate neurons divide the preplate into a superficial marginal zone (layer I) and a deep subplate.

test.q: Which transcription factor is the classic marker of layer V subcerebral neurons?
test.explain: CTIP2 (BCL11B) marks layer V neurons that project to the spinal cord and brainstem. SATB2 and CUX2 mark upper layers, and TBR1 marks layer VI.

test.q: What happens to layering in the reeler mouse, which lacks Reelin?
choices: Layer I is much thicker than usual
Layers form normally but more slowly
test.explain: Without Reelin the preplate fails to split, and the layers end up roughly outside-in.

test.q: Reelin signals through VLDLR and ApoER2 to phosphorylate which protein?
test.explain: Reelin binding triggers phosphorylation of the adaptor protein DAB1.

test.q: Layer II/III neurons mainly send their axons to which targets?
test.explain: Upper-layer neurons make corticocortical and callosal connections. Layer V projects to the spinal cord, and layer VI to the thalamus.

test.q: Mutations in RELN or VLDLR in humans cause which condition?
test.explain: Disrupted Reelin signaling causes a smooth cortex with an underdeveloped cerebellum.

test.q: What is the term for the generation of new neurons from progenitor cells?
test.explain: Neurogenesis produces neurons. In human cortex it happens mostly in the first half of pregnancy.

test.q: The cortex is built ___-out, with new neurons passing older ones.
test.explain: Inside-out layering means each new cohort settles more superficially than the last.

test.q: How many layers does the mammalian neocortex have?
test.explain: The neocortex has six layers, numbered I to VI from the surface inward.

kidTest.q: How many layers does the brain's outer part have?
kidTest.explain: The cortex has six layers, like a six-layer cake.

kidTest.q: Where do the first brain cells made end up?
kidTest.explain: The first cells stay deep. Newer cells climb past them.

kidTest.q: What do newer cells do to reach their spot?
choices: Wait for old cells to leave
kidTest.explain: New cells move up past the older ones and settle on top.

kidTest.q: Cells made later in building become which layers?
kidTest.explain: Later cells end up closer to the outside.

kidTest.q: The brain's wrinkly outer layer is called the c _ _ _ _ x.
kidTest.explain: The cortex is the brain's layered outer part.

advancedTest.q: Late ferret progenitors transplanted into young hosts did not make deep-layer neurons. This best supports:
choices: Separate lineages for upper and lower layers from the start
Fate set by the host environment after migration ends
Progressive restriction of progenitor competence over time
Reelin signaling as the main factor setting neuron identity
advancedTest.explain: Late progenitors had lost the ability to make deep fates even in a young environment. This shows competence narrows over time and is not set by the environment alone.

advancedTest.q: Misplaced neurons in the reeler mouse keep birthdate-appropriate markers and projections. What does this imply?
choices: Upper-layer neurons are produced before deep-layer ones
Neuronal identity and laminar position can be uncoupled
Laminar position is what determines molecular identity
Reelin acts mainly by specifying transcription factor codes
advancedTest.explain: Identity tracks birthdate rather than final position. Positioning (Reelin) and fate specification are separable processes.

advancedTest.q: Human cortex has a far larger share of supragranular neurons than mouse. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Shortened G1 phase producing more deep-layer neurons
Extra Cajal-Retzius cells expanding the marginal zone
Prolonged neurogenesis with OSVZ amplification late
Reversal to outside-in layering in the primate cortex
advancedTest.explain: A longer neurogenic period and outer subventricular zone progenitors expand the late-born upper layers.

advancedTest.q: Why does an earlier-gestation Zika or CMV infection tend to cause more severe cortical malformation?
choices: It mainly affects Cajal-Retzius cells in layer I
It strikes progenitors before most neurons exist
It acts mainly by blocking myelination afterward
It spares progenitors and targets mature neurons
advancedTest.explain: Injuring progenitors early removes the source of many later cohorts. Timing determines which neuron populations are lost.

lessons.title: Radial and Tangential Neuronal Migration

levels.kid:
Your brain's outer layer, the cortex, is built from billions of nerve cells. But most of them are not born where they end up. They have to travel!

Many new cells climb straight up, like a climber on a **rope**. The ropes are long, thin helper cells that stretch from the inside of the brain to the outside. Each new cell grabs a rope and climbs to its spot.

Other cells, the brain's "calm-down" cells, are born far away. They walk **sideways** across the brain, like kids crossing a playground, to find their place.

A stop signal at the top tells cells where to stop. If cells get stuck on the way, the brain's surface can end up too smooth, and the brain may not work the way it should.
levels.hs:
**Neuronal migration** is the journey new neurons make from where they are born to where they will work. In the cerebral cortex, there are two main routes.

**Radial migration** carries **excitatory neurons** (pyramidal neurons, which use the neurotransmitter glutamate). They are born near the fluid-filled ventricles deep in the brain and move outward toward the surface. They travel along **radial glia**, stem cells with long fibers stretching from the ventricle to the brain's surface, like climbing a rope. Each new wave of neurons climbs past the older ones, building the layers from the inside out.

**Tangential migration** carries **inhibitory interneurons** (which use GABA). They are born outside the cortex, in bulges of the lower forebrain called the **ganglionic eminences**, then travel sideways, parallel to the brain surface, over long distances before turning into the cortex.

Neurons need signals to start, steer and stop. A protein called **Reelin**, made by **Cajal-Retzius cells** near the surface, helps neurons know where to stop.

Real example: in **lissencephaly** ("smooth brain"), neurons fail to migrate properly, so the cortex is thick and lacks normal folds. Children often have severe developmental delay and seizures. One common cause is a mutation in the gene **LIS1**, which helps move the cell's nucleus forward during migration.
levels.college:
**Radial migration** of pyramidal neurons proceeds in stages:
- Newborn neurons leave the ventricular and subventricular zones and pause in the intermediate zone as **multipolar cells**, extending and retracting many short processes and wandering slowly.
- They then convert to a **bipolar** shape, with a leading process toward the pia and a trailing process that becomes the axon. They attach to radial glial fibers and migrate by **locomotion**.
- Near the top, the leading process anchors in the marginal zone and the cell body pulls itself up by **terminal somal translocation**, passing older neurons (inside-out order). The earliest neurons, when the wall is thin, move only by somal translocation.

Locomotion is a **two-stroke cycle**: the leading process extends, a swelling forms ahead of the nucleus, the **centrosome** moves into it, then the nucleus is pulled forward (**nucleokinesis**) by **dynein** along microtubules, helped by actomyosin contraction at the rear. **LIS1** regulates dynein; **doublecortin (DCX)** stabilizes microtubules.

**Reelin**, secreted by Cajal-Retzius cells, binds **VLDLR** and **ApoER2**, triggering phosphorylation of the adaptor **Dab1**. This signal promotes detachment from glia and correct positioning. The **reeler** mouse, which lacks Reelin, has a roughly inverted cortex.

**Tangential migration** of GABAergic interneurons:
- About 60-70% arise from the **medial ganglionic eminence** (MGE, transcription factor **Nkx2.1**; parvalbumin and somatostatin types), about 30% from the **caudal ganglionic eminence** (CGE), and a few from the preoptic area. **Dlx** genes are needed for their migration.
- They avoid the striatum (repelled by semaphorins via neuropilins), enter the cortex in two streams, in the marginal zone and the lower intermediate/subventricular zone, held there by **CXCL12** acting on **CXCR4**, then dive radially into the cortical plate.
- Neuregulin-1 attracts them via the receptor **ErbB4**.
levels.phd:
Classic evidence for glia-guided migration came from **Rakic (1972)**, whose serial electron micrographs of fetal macaque cortex showed neurons wrapped around radial glial fibers across a long intermediate zone. Tangential migration of interneurons was established in the late 1990s by **Anderson, Rubenstein and colleagues**: **Dlx1/2** double mutants lose most cortical GABAergic cells, and slice tracing showed cells streaming from the ganglionic eminences into the pallium. In humans and primates, a subset of interneurons may also arise in dorsal progenitors, but the ventral origin predominates.

**Mechanics.** Locomoting neurons couple a leading-process "cytoplasmic dilation" with centrosome advance, then nuclear translocation via **LIS1-NDEL1-dynein** pulling on a perinuclear microtubule cage, coupled to the nuclear envelope by **LINC complexes** (SUN/nesprin). Myosin II contraction at the rear contributes. **DCX** and **TUBA1A** tune microtubule dynamics. **Filamin A** (actin crosslinking) is needed to start migration, and its loss leaves neurons at the ventricle (**periventricular nodular heterotopia**). The multipolar-to-bipolar transition depends on **Cdk5** with its activator **p35**, and on RhoA/Rac1 signaling.

**Reelin signaling** is the best-characterized stop/position pathway. Reelin binding to **VLDLR/ApoER2** clusters receptors and activates **Src-family kinases (Fyn)** to tyrosine-phosphorylate **Dab1**, recruiting PI3K/Akt, Crk/C3G-Rap1 and N-cadherin trafficking. Rap1-driven N-cadherin upregulation helps orient multipolar cells and later anchors the leading process during terminal translocation. Dab1 knockouts and VLDLR/ApoER2 double knockouts phenocopy **reeler**, showing these components act in one linear pathway. Whether Reelin is a stop signal, a detach signal or a permissive orienting cue remains debated; it likely serves different roles at different stages.

**Interneuron guidance** integrates motogenic factors (HGF, BDNF/GDNF), repulsion from the striatum (Sema3A/3F via neuropilins) and from the eminence (Slit/Robo), attraction toward the cortex (Nrg1 type III and Ig-Nrg1 via ErbB4) and stream maintenance by **CXCL12/CXCR4/CXCR7**. Cxcr4 loss causes premature exit from streams into the cortical plate and abnormal laminar distribution. Interneurons migrate with a branched leading process, choosing the direction by stabilizing one branch.
levels.expert:
Migration defects are a major bridge from neurodevelopmental cell biology to the clinic, and the imaging pattern often points to the pathway.

**Genotype-imaging correlation:**
- **PAFAH1B1 (LIS1)** heterozygous loss causes lissencephaly that is worse posteriorly (posterior > anterior gradient); a larger 17p13.3 deletion including YWHAE gives **Miller-Dieker syndrome**, with facial dysmorphism.
- **DCX** (X-linked) gives anterior-predominant lissencephaly in males and **subcortical band heterotopia** in heterozygous females, as random X-inactivation leaves a population of neurons that stall and form a "double cortex."
- **RELN** and **VLDLR** recessive mutations cause lissencephaly with marked **cerebellar hypoplasia**, reflecting Reelin's role in Purkinje cell positioning.
- **ARX** loss causes X-linked lissencephaly with abnormal genitalia (XLAG), combining radial defects with failed interneuron migration; ARX variants also cause infantile epileptic spasms without malformation.
- **Tubulinopathies** (TUBA1A, TUBB2B, TUBB3) mix lissencephaly or polymicrogyria-like cortex with basal ganglia and corpus callosum anomalies.

For epilepsy surgery, heterotopia matter because seizures may arise from networks linking heterotopic gray matter and overlying cortex; stereo-EEG and laser ablation of nodules are used in selected patients. Diffuse lissencephaly is generally not a resection candidate.

**Interneuronopathy** is a working hypothesis linking disrupted tangential migration to epilepsy, schizophrenia and autism (for example via ErbB4, NRG1 and CXCR4 pathway variants), though human causal evidence is uneven.

**Recent human data:** Paredes and colleagues (2016) described an "Arc" of young GABAergic neurons streaming into the infant frontal lobe for months after birth. This suggests postnatal shaping of prefrontal inhibition and a window of vulnerability, for example to neonatal hypoxia or prematurity. Sanai et al. (2011) showed that a medial migratory stream branching from the infant rostral migratory stream feeds the ventromedial prefrontal cortex.

**Tools and open questions:** cortical organoids and assembloids (dorsal-ventral fusions) let researchers film patient-derived interneurons migrating; LIS1 patient organoids show altered radial glia and slowed migration. Open issues include how outer radial glia scaffolds in the folded human cortex alter migration paths, and whether drugs aimed at the cytoskeleton could ever rescue migration after birth.

keyPoints: Excitatory pyramidal neurons migrate radially along radial glial fibers
Inhibitory interneurons migrate tangentially from the ganglionic eminences (MGE, CGE)
Locomotion uses a two-stroke cycle: centrosome advances, dynein pulls the nucleus
Reelin from Cajal-Retzius cells signals via VLDLR/ApoER2 and Dab1 to position neurons
LIS1, DCX, filamin A and tubulin mutations cause lissencephaly and heterotopia
CXCL12/CXCR4 keeps interneurons in streams; Nrg1/ErbB4 attracts them to cortex

test.q: What structure guides excitatory neurons during radial migration?
test.explain: Pyramidal neurons climb along the long fibers of radial glia, which stretch from the ventricle to the pial surface.

test.q: Where are most cortical GABAergic interneurons born?
test.explain: Most interneurons arise in the medial and caudal ganglionic eminences of the ventral forebrain, then migrate tangentially into the cortex.

test.q: How do excitatory pyramidal neurons reach the cortical plate?
choices: Radially from the dorsal ventricular zone
test.explain: Pyramidal neurons are born in the dorsal (pallial) ventricular and subventricular zones and move outward radially. Tangential routes are used by interneurons.

test.q: Which cells secrete Reelin in the marginal zone?
test.explain: Cajal-Retzius cells near the pial surface secrete Reelin, which helps neurons detach from glia and settle in position.

test.q: Tangentially migrating cortical interneurons mainly use which neurotransmitter?
test.explain: Interneurons are inhibitory and use GABA; radially migrating pyramidal neurons use glutamate.

test.q: LIS1 regulates which motor protein that pulls the nucleus forward?
test.explain: LIS1 works with dynein to pull the nucleus along microtubules during nucleokinesis. Myosin II contributes rear contraction but is not LIS1's partner.

test.q: Before attaching to radial glia, many new neurons in the intermediate zone are:
test.explain: New neurons pause as multipolar cells, then convert to a bipolar shape and begin glia-guided locomotion.

test.q: Females with a heterozygous DCX mutation typically show which malformation?
test.explain: Because of X-inactivation, some neurons express the mutant DCX and stall, forming a band of gray matter beneath the cortex (double cortex). Periventricular nodules are typical of filamin A loss.

test.q: The chemokine CXCL12 keeps interneurons in their migratory streams by acting on:
test.explain: CXCL12 signals through CXCR4 (and CXCR7). ErbB4 is the neuregulin receptor; VLDLR is a Reelin receptor.

test.q: Which transcription factor marks the medial ganglionic eminence that produces parvalbumin and somatostatin interneurons?
test.explain: Nkx2.1 specifies MGE identity, the source of about 60-70% of cortical interneurons.

test.q: The mouse mutant lacking Reelin, whose cortical layers are roughly inverted, is called ___.
test.explain: Reeler mice lack Reelin; Dab1 and VLDLR/ApoER2 mutants look the same.

test.q: What mode of migration lets a neuron keep its leading process anchored at the pia and pull its cell body upward?
test.explain: Early neurons and the final step of later neurons use somal translocation instead of glia-guided locomotion.

kidTest.q: What do many new brain cells climb along?
kidTest.explain: Long thin helper cells act like ropes that new cells climb.

kidTest.q: How do the brain's "calm-down" cells travel?
kidTest.explain: They are born far away and walk sideways across the brain.

kidTest.q: If many cells get stuck on the way, the brain's surface may be:
kidTest.explain: When cells don't arrive, the brain doesn't fold normally and looks too smooth.

kidTest.q: What tells traveling cells where to stop?
choices: A stop signal at the top
kidTest.explain: A signal near the brain's surface tells cells when to stop.

kidTest.q: New cells climb helper fibers like a climber on a r _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The helper fibers work like ropes for climbing cells.

advancedTest.q: Mice lacking Dab1, or lacking both VLDLR and ApoER2, look like reeler. Best inference?
choices: Reelin signals via the receptors to Dab1 in one series
Dab1 is a guidance cue released by radial glial fibers
Reelin mainly controls interneuron birth in the MGE
VLDLR and ApoER2 are secreted by Cajal-Retzius cells
advancedTest.explain: Identical phenotypes from losing ligand, receptors or adaptor indicate a single linear pathway: Reelin binds VLDLR/ApoER2, leading to Dab1 phosphorylation.

advancedTest.q: Why does a heterozygous DCX mutation in females produce a band of heterotopic gray matter plus a near-normal cortex?
choices: Mutant DCX is toxic mainly to cortical interneurons
Neurons expressing the mutant X stall beneath cortex
Radial glia fail to form in half of the hemispheres
Interneurons from the MGE stay inside the eminence
advancedTest.explain: Random X-inactivation creates two neuron populations: those using the normal X migrate correctly, those using the mutant X arrest and form the subcortical band.

advancedTest.q: Streams of young GABAergic neurons enter the infant frontal lobe for months after birth. What is the most reasonable implication?
choices: Pyramidal neurons are mostly born after birth
Radial glia keep making neurons into adulthood
Frontal inhibition is shaped partly after birth
The rostral migratory stream ends in the cerebellum
advancedTest.explain: Late interneuron arrival means frontal inhibitory circuits are still being assembled postnatally, creating a window of vulnerability, for example to prematurity.

advancedTest.q: In Cxcr4 mutant mice, interneurons leave their tangential streams early and enter the cortical plate. Best explanation?
choices: They lose Nrg1 attraction from the cortex
They lose a signal holding them in the streams
They are repelled by Reelin in the marginal zone
They become excitatory and switch to radial migration
advancedTest.explain: CXCL12 acting on CXCR4 maintains interneurons in the marginal and subventricular streams; without it they dive into the cortical plate prematurely, causing abnormal laminar distribution.

lessons.title: Axon Guidance: Netrins, Slits, Semaphorins and Ephrins

levels.kid:
When a baby's brain is growing, each nerve cell sends out a long wire called an **axon**. The axon has to find the right partner, sometimes far away. How does it know where to go?

The tip of the axon is like a tiny hand with fingers. It feels the path as it crawls along. Along the way there are chemical signs. Some signs say "come this way!" Others say "stay away!"

Scientists gave these signs names like **netrins**, **slits**, **semaphorins** and **ephrins**. Netrin is often a "come here" sign. Slit is often a "keep out" sign.

By following the signs, billions of axons connect the right places, a bit like cars following road signs to the right town.
levels.hs:
Neurons connect over long distances by growing an **axon**, a long cable that carries signals. During development, the axon's tip forms a **growth cone**, a moving, hand-shaped structure with finger-like **filopodia** that sense chemicals around it.

Guidance signals come in two kinds:
- **Attractants** pull the growth cone toward them.
- **Repellents** push it away.
They can act at short range (stuck to cells) or long range (spreading out as a gradient).

Four classic families of guidance molecules:
- **Netrins**: often attract axons, for example toward the midline of the spinal cord.
- **Slits**: repel axons through **Robo** receptors.
- **Semaphorins**: mostly repel, causing the growth cone to collapse.
- **Ephrins**: bind **Eph receptors** on neighbouring cells, sorting axons into orderly maps.

A classic example is **midline crossing**. Many axons in the spinal cord must cross from one side to the other. Netrin from the floor plate (the midline) attracts them. Once across, they become sensitive to Slit, which pushes them away so they never wander back. This is part of why the left brain controls the right side of the body.

When guidance fails, wiring goes wrong. In one rare inherited disorder, a mutation in a Robo gene means brainstem axons fail to cross properly, which affects eye movements.
levels.college:
The **growth cone** converts extracellular cues into directed movement by reorganizing its cytoskeleton: actin in filopodia and lamellipodia, microtubules in the central domain. Attractive cues promote actin polymerization on the near side; repulsive cues trigger local depolymerization or collapse. The same cue can attract or repel depending on the receptors present and on internal second messengers.

The four canonical families:
- **Netrin-1** (a laminin-related secreted protein) attracts via **DCC**. Signaling through **UNC5** receptors, alone or with DCC, causes repulsion.
- **Slits** (Slit1-3) are secreted by the midline and repel via **Robo1/2**. Robo3 regulates midline crossing.
- **Semaphorins** are over 20 secreted or membrane-bound proteins. Secreted class 3 semaphorins (e.g., Sema3A) signal through **neuropilin-plexin** complexes; plexins act as GAPs for Ras-family GTPases, and downstream CRMP/cofilin changes drive collapse.
- **Ephrins**: ephrin-A (GPI-anchored) binds EphA; ephrin-B (transmembrane) binds EphB. Signaling is **bidirectional**: both cells respond. Graded EphA/ephrin-A expression maps retinal axons onto the tectum/superior colliculus, the molecular basis of Sperry's **chemoaffinity hypothesis**.

**Midline switching** in commissural axons: before crossing, Robo3.1 blunts Slit repulsion and netrin/DCC attraction dominates. At the floor plate, Robo3 is downregulated and Robo1/2 rise, so Slit expels the axon and prevents recrossing. Sonic hedgehog also acts as a midline attractant.

In the cortex, these cues shape the **corpus callosum** (with glial guidepost structures such as the indusium griseum glia and midline zipper glia), corticospinal tract decussation in the medulla, and thalamocortical projections. Rho GTPases (RhoA, Rac1, Cdc42) are the common final pathway linking receptors to the cytoskeleton.
levels.phd:
Growth cone steering is a problem of signal amplification. Filopodia detect concentration differences across the growth cone, probably around 1-2%. These differences are amplified by Ca2+ and cyclic nucleotide signaling. Poo and colleagues showed in Xenopus spinal neurons that netrin-1 attraction converts to repulsion when cAMP/PKA activity is lowered. The cGMP:cAMP ratio similarly tunes Sema3A responses. Local **translation** in growth cones matters too: netrin-1 triggers β-actin synthesis on the near side, while Sema3A and Slit induce RhoA and cofilin translation (Holt lab), although how much local translation is required remains debated.

Key discoveries:
- Netrins were purified from embryonic chick brain by Tessier-Lavigne and colleagues (1994) as floor-plate chemoattractants. They are orthologous to *C. elegans* UNC-6.
- Robo was identified in Drosophila *roundabout* mutants, in which axons cross the midline repeatedly. Slit was confirmed as its ligand (1999).
- In Drosophila, Commissureless sorts Robo away from the surface before crossing. In vertebrates, Robo3.1 plays the analogous anti-repulsive role.

Netrin-1's status as a long-range diffusible gradient has been revised. Floor-plate-specific deletion barely affects commissural guidance in the hindbrain and spinal cord (Dominici et al., 2017; Varadarajan et al., 2017). Ventricular zone progenitors deposit netrin-1 on pial radial-glial endfeet, where it acts haptotactically at short range.

Semaphorin signaling: Sema3A binds Nrp1, which recruits PlexinA. Plexin cytoplasmic GAP activity inactivates R-Ras/Rap1, reducing integrin adhesion. Fyn/Cdk5 phosphorylate CRMP2, destabilizing microtubules. Eph-ephrin contact creates an adhesion problem, since binding should glue cells together. It is resolved by ADAM10 cleavage of ephrin or by trans-endocytosis of the receptor-ligand complex.

Diversity is multiplied by co-receptors (DSCAM, neogenin) and by Robo-DCC cross-silencing (Stein & Tessier-Lavigne 2001). Responsiveness also changes over time through proteolysis and endocytic trafficking. Topographic mapping needs gradient matching plus competition between axons and activity-dependent refinement. Ephrin gradients alone do not fully explain retinocollicular maps, as relative-signaling knock-in experiments (Brown et al., 2000, Isl2-EphA3) showed.
levels.expert:
Clinically, guidance defects show up as **miswiring disorders**, increasingly grouped as "developmental axon guidance disorders" or neuronal connectivity disorders.

- **Horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis (HGPPS)**: biallelic *ROBO3* mutations. Corticospinal and dorsal-column-lemniscal pathways fail to decussate, giving ipsilateral motor and sensory representation. Diffusion tractography and TMS show uncrossed tracts. MRI features include a split pons and a butterfly-shaped medulla.
- **Congenital mirror movements**: heterozygous *DCC* (also *RAD51*, *NTN1*) variants cause bilateral corticospinal projections. Some *DCC* variants instead cause agenesis of the corpus callosum, with or without horizontal gaze palsy.
- **Joubert syndrome** (a ciliopathy) produces the molar tooth sign and absent decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles. It shows how non-guidance genes can disrupt guidance indirectly through cilia-dependent Shh signaling.
- **Kallmann syndrome** (*ANOS1*, *FGFR1*, *SEMA3A*, *PLXNA1*) links olfactory axon and GnRH neuron migration defects.
- **Congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders**: Duane syndrome (*CHN1*, α2-chimaerin, a Rac-GAP acting downstream of EphA4) and CFEOM (*KIF21A*, *TUBB3*). They are classic examples of motor axons reaching the wrong muscles.

Pitfalls: agenesis of the corpus callosum is genetically heterogeneous, with hundreds of associated genes. Isolated ACC on fetal MRI often has a good outcome, but missing associated anomalies changes counselling. Variant interpretation in guidance genes is hard, because many alleles have incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity.

Translational relevance for neurosurgery: the same cues are reused as **barriers to regeneration** in the adult CNS. Sema3A in the fibrotic scar, ephrin-B3/EphA4 in myelin and around injury sites, and RGM all inhibit regrowth. A Sema3A inhibitor improved regeneration in rodent spinal cord injury models. Anti-RGMa antibodies (elezanumab) reached human trials in spinal cord injury and stroke without clear efficacy so far. Guidance molecules also matter in neuro-oncology: netrin/UNC5 and DCC act as "dependence receptors" that trigger apoptosis when unliganded, and Slit-Robo and semaphorins influence glioma invasion and angiogenesis.

Open questions: how a limited set of cue families specifies trillions of connections (combinatorial codes, isoforms, timing); the reliability of tractography for detecting subtle miswiring in neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism; and whether guidance pathways can be safely reactivated in adults.

keyPoints: The axon's growth cone senses attractive and repulsive cues to steer
Netrin-1 attracts via DCC; UNC5 receptors mediate repulsion
Slits repel via Robo receptors and stop axons from recrossing the midline
Semaphorins signal through neuropilin-plexin to collapse growth cones
Ephrin-Eph signaling is bidirectional and builds topographic maps
Guidance gene mutations cause miswiring, e.g., ROBO3 in HGPPS and DCC in mirror movements

test.q: What is the motile structure at the tip of a growing axon called?
test.explain: The growth cone senses cues and steers the axon. The axon hillock is where action potentials begin.

test.q: Which receptor mediates netrin-1 attraction?
test.explain: DCC (Deleted in Colorectal Cancer) mediates attraction. UNC5 mediates repulsion.

test.q: Slit proteins repel axons mainly by binding which receptors?
test.explain: Slit-Robo signaling repels axons from the midline.

test.q: After crossing the midline, why don't commissural axons cross back?
choices: They gain Slit sensitivity via Robo1/2
test.explain: Robo3 falls and Robo1/2 rise after crossing, so midline Slit expels the axon.

test.q: Class 3 semaphorins like Sema3A signal through which receptor complex?
test.explain: Sema3A binds neuropilin-1, which recruits a plexin-A signaling subunit.

test.q: What makes ephrin-Eph signaling unusual?
choices: It signals into both contacting cells
It operates in adult cells alone
It acts over very long distances
test.explain: Ephrins and Ephs are membrane-bound, and signaling runs both forward and reverse.

test.q: Graded EphA/ephrin-A expression mapping retina onto the colliculus supports which idea?
test.explain: Sperry proposed that molecular tags guide axons to their targets. Ephrin gradients are a key example.

test.q: Which proteins link guidance receptors to cytoskeleton changes?
test.explain: RhoA, Rac1 and Cdc42 act as a common pathway controlling actin dynamics.

test.q: In HGPPS, which gene is mutated so that major tracts fail to cross?
test.explain: Biallelic ROBO3 mutations prevent normal midline crossing.

test.q: Which family of secreted guidance cues, orthologous to worm UNC-6, attracts axons to the floor plate?
test.explain: Netrins were purified as floor-plate chemoattractants.

test.q: The fly mutant whose axons cross the midline repeatedly is called ___.
test.explain: Roundabout (Robo) mutants revealed the Slit receptor.

test.q: Heterozygous DCC variants can cause congenital ___ movements.
test.explain: Bilateral corticospinal projections make one hand copy the other's movements.

kidTest.q: What is the long wire a nerve cell grows?
kidTest.explain: The axon carries messages to other cells.

kidTest.q: What does the axon tip use to find its way?
kidTest.explain: It follows chemical 'come here' and 'stay away' signs.

kidTest.q: Netrin is often what kind of sign?
choices: A sign that puts cells to sleep
A sign that repels growing axons
kidTest.explain: Netrin often attracts axons, acting as a come-here sign for growing nerve fibers.

kidTest.q: Slit is often what kind of sign?
kidTest.explain: Slit pushes axons away.

kidTest.q: The axon tip is like a tiny h _ _ _ with fingers.
kidTest.explain: The growth cone feels its way like a hand.

advancedTest.q: Lowering cAMP/PKA in Xenopus growth cones turns netrin-1 attraction into repulsion. What does this show?
choices: Internal second messengers set the sign of the cue response
Repulsion requires the floor plate to secrete Slit
PKA directly degrades the DCC receptor protein
Netrin-1 binds a different receptor when cAMP is low
advancedTest.explain: The same cue and receptor can give opposite turning depending on cyclic nucleotide state.

advancedTest.q: Floor-plate-specific netrin-1 deletion barely affects commissural guidance. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Progenitor-derived netrin-1 on pial endfeet guides at short range
Netrin-1 plays little role in commissural axon guidance
Slit takes over as the main midline attractant
DCC signals without binding any ligand
advancedTest.explain: Ventricular zone progenitors deposit netrin-1 that acts haptotactically, revising the long-range gradient model.

advancedTest.q: Eph-ephrin binding is high-affinity yet yields repulsion. How is detachment achieved?
choices: Receptor phosphatases prevent further ligand binding
Calcium influx dissolves the plasma membrane locally
Ephrins become secreted once cells touch
ADAM10 cleavage or trans-endocytosis of the complex
advancedTest.explain: Proteolytic shedding or trans-endocytosis removes the adhesive complex, allowing retraction.

advancedTest.q: Why are guidance cues relevant to adult spinal cord injury therapy?
choices: They are absent from the adult nervous system
They mainly promote myelination of new axons
They primarily control neuronal cell division
Cues like Sema3A and RGMa inhibit regrowth after injury
advancedTest.explain: Developmental repellents are re-expressed around injury sites. Blocking them, for example with an anti-RGMa antibody, has been tested to promote regeneration.

lessons.title: Synaptogenesis, Pruning and the Myelination Timeline

levels.kid:
Your brain cells talk to each other at tiny meeting spots called **synapses**. When you were a baby, your brain built these meeting spots super fast, like a city building thousands of new roads every second.

But too many roads make traffic messy. So, as you grow, your brain removes roads nobody uses. This is called **pruning**, just like a gardener trimming a bush so it grows strong. The roads you use a lot, like the ones for reading or riding a bike, get kept.

The brain also wraps its wires in a fatty coat called **myelin**. It works like the plastic around a phone charger cord, and it makes messages zoom faster. The back of the brain gets wrapped first. The front, which helps you plan, finishes last, in your twenties!
levels.hs:
A **synapse** is the junction where one neuron passes a signal to another, usually by releasing chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. Building synapses is called **synaptogenesis**. In the human cortex it starts before birth and explodes in the first years of life. At its peak, a toddler's cortex has far more synapses than an adult's.

Next comes **synaptic pruning**: the brain removes weak or unused synapses and strengthens busy ones. The rule is "use it or lose it." Neurons that fire together keep their connection. Pruning makes circuits more efficient. It happens at different times in different areas:
- Visual cortex: synapses peak in the first year, and pruning follows in early childhood.
- Prefrontal cortex (planning, self-control): synapses peak later and pruning continues through adolescence.

**Myelination** is the wrapping of axons (the neuron's output wires) in **myelin**, a fatty insulating layer. In the brain, cells called **oligodendrocytes** make myelin. Myelin can speed signals up by more than 50 times. It begins before birth in the brainstem, spreads to sensory and motor areas in infancy, and finishes last in the prefrontal cortex, in the mid-twenties.

Real example: in the 1960s and 70s, Hubel and Wiesel showed that if one eye of a young kitten is covered, connections from that eye to the visual cortex shrink. The other eye takes over. This only happens during a **critical period** early in life.
levels.college:
Cortical circuits form in three overlapping phases: synapse formation, activity-dependent refinement, and myelination.

**Synaptogenesis.** When a growth cone contacts its target, adhesion molecules organize both sides of the synapse:
- **Neurexins** (presynaptic) bind **neuroligins** (postsynaptic) and recruit scaffolds such as PSD-95.
- Other organizers include SynCAMs, LRRTMs, and secreted factors from astrocytes (thrombospondins, glypicans).
- Many early glutamatergic synapses are **silent**: they contain NMDA receptors but lack AMPA receptors. Activity inserts AMPA receptors and switches them on.
- Early on, GABA is depolarizing because immature neurons have high internal chloride. This changes as KCC2 expression rises around birth.

Peter Huttenlocher counted synapses in postmortem human cortex. Synaptic density peaks around 8 months in visual cortex and around 1-3 years or later in prefrontal cortex. It then declines, by roughly 40-50% in prefrontal cortex by late adolescence.

**Pruning.** Synapses compete. Correlated activity stabilizes a synapse through NMDA receptor-dependent Hebbian plasticity. Weak synapses are tagged and removed:
- Complement proteins **C1q** and **C3** coat weak synapses.
- **Microglia** carry the complement receptor CR3 and engulf the tagged synapses.
- Astrocytes also prune, using the receptors MEGF10 and MERTK.

**Critical periods.** Ocular dominance plasticity depends on GABAergic **parvalbumin interneurons** maturing. Perineuronal nets and myelin-associated signals such as Nogo receptor later close the window.

**Myelination.** Oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) differentiate and wrap axons. This enables **saltatory conduction** between nodes of Ranvier. Flechsig described the order: caudal to rostral, central to peripheral, and sensory before motor before association areas. Major milestones:
- Brainstem and posterior limb of the internal capsule: near term.
- Corpus callosum splenium by about 6 months, genu by about 8 months.
- Adult-like appearance on T1 MRI by about 1 year and on T2 by about 2 years.
- Association fibers continue into the third decade.
levels.phd:
**Synapse specification.** Synaptic organizers act combinatorially. The **neurexin** genes NRXN1-3 use alternative promoters and splice sites (such as SS4) to generate thousands of isoforms. These isoforms bind different partners: neuroligins, LRRTMs, and cerebellin-GluD2 complexes. Neuroligin-1 favors excitatory synapses and neuroligin-2 favors inhibitory ones. Knockout studies by Südhof's group showed that neurexins and neuroligins are needed for synapses to *function* properly, more than for synapses to form at all. Astrocytes add another layer: thrombospondins acting through α2δ-1 make structural but silent synapses, and glypican-4/6 and SPARCL1 recruit AMPA receptors.

**The developmental GABA shift.** Immature neurons express NKCC1 and little KCC2, so internal chloride is high and GABA depolarizes them. This drives giant depolarizing potentials and helps synapses mature. The timing of the switch around birth (Ben-Ari) and whether the effect is truly excitatory in vivo remain debated.

**Pruning mechanisms.** Stevens, Barres and colleagues showed that in the developing retinogeniculate system, C1q and C3 localize to less active synapses and microglia engulf them via CR3. In mice lacking these molecules, eye-specific segregation is incomplete. Other signals adjust this process:
- Fractalkine (CX3CR1) and TREM2 also shape pruning.
- CD47-SIRPα acts as a "don't eat me" signal that protects active inputs.
- MHC class I and PirB limit plasticity.
- Exposed phosphatidylserine acts as an "eat me" tag.

Sekar et al. (2016) linked **schizophrenia** risk to structural variants of complement **C4A**, which increase C4A expression and plausibly drive excessive adolescent pruning. Postmortem studies of autism show reduced spine pruning together with mTOR hyperactivity and impaired autophagy (Tang et al., 2014).

**Myelination biology.** OPCs arise in waves, and the late cortical wave persists into adulthood. Myelin regulatory factor (MYRF), SOX10 and OLIG2 drive differentiation. Neuronal activity promotes myelination, which is called **adaptive myelination** (Gibson et al., 2014, using optogenetics). Myelin is not purely static insulation:
- Internode length and periaxonal metabolic support (oligodendrocyte lactate via MCT1) tune conduction timing.
- Proteomic studies show this support sustains axon health.

Diffusion MRI shows fractional anisotropy rising nonlinearly through the twenties. Cortical gray matter thinning in adolescence reflects both pruning and myelin encroachment, and these two are hard to separate with imaging.
levels.expert:
**Clinical reading of myelination.** Neuroradiologists judge maturity against milestones, and the sequence of signal change matters as much as the timing:
- T1 hyperintensity appears first, and T2 hypointensity lags by months.
- A child aged around two years with persistent T2-bright, unmyelinated white matter suggests **hypomyelination**.
- Hypomyelination has different causes than demyelination or delay: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease (PLP1), POLR3-related leukodystrophy, and 18q deletion (MBP).
- Terminal zones of the peritrigonal white matter can stay T2-bright into the second decade. Do not call this periventricular leukomalacia.
- Preterm infants should be assessed by corrected age.

**Prematurity.** Late OPCs (pre-oligodendrocytes, about 23-32 weeks) are very vulnerable to hypoxia-ischemia and inflammation. This underlies diffuse white matter injury. Arrest of maturation, with OPCs that fail to differentiate, rather than cell loss, now dominates the model. That has motivated trials of remyelination-promoting strategies, whose results so far are mixed.

**Synaptopathies in the clinic.** Many neurodevelopmental genes act at the synapse:
- SHANK3 (Phelan-McDermid syndrome).
- NRXN1 deletions, which are pleiotropic risk factors for autism, intellectual disability, schizophrenia and epilepsy.
- NLGN3/4X, SYNGAP1, and the fragile X protein FMRP.

The mGluR theory of fragile X looked compelling in mice, but mGluR5 antagonist trials failed in humans. Likely reasons include poor outcome measures, testing at an age when critical windows may have closed, and differences between species. This is a central caution for anyone translating synaptic biology into therapy.

**Reopening plasticity.** Experimental approaches try to reopen critical periods:
- Removing perineuronal nets (chondroitinase).
- Blocking Lynx1 or Nogo receptor.
- Dark exposure in amblyopia models.

Clinically, amblyopia treatment works best in childhood but retains some adult efficacy, for example with dichoptic binocular therapy.

**Complement in disease.** The same microglia-complement machinery reactivates in Alzheimer disease, glaucoma and multiple sclerosis, leading to synapse loss. Anti-C1q antibodies are in clinical development, which raises a developmental-safety question for pediatric use.

**Open questions.** Is pruning in human adolescence driven mainly by microglia, by astrocytes, or by cell-intrinsic processes? Can MRI separate synapse loss from myelin gain? And how much does activity-dependent myelination contribute to learning and recovery after surgery or injury? This last question is directly relevant to neurosurgical rehabilitation.

keyPoints: Synaptogenesis peaks in early childhood, earlier in visual than in prefrontal cortex
Neurexin-neuroligin binding and astrocyte factors organize new synapses
Pruning removes weak synapses: complement tags them and microglia engulf them
Critical periods (Hubel and Wiesel) need experience and close as interneurons mature
Oligodendrocytes myelinate from caudal to rostral; prefrontal cortex finishes in the mid-20s
Synapse and myelin disorders include autism genes, schizophrenia (C4A) and hypomyelination

test.q: Which cells make myelin in the central nervous system?
test.explain: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons. Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves.

test.q: Which cortical region reaches peak synaptic density earliest?
test.explain: Huttenlocher found that visual cortex peaks around 8 months, while prefrontal cortex peaks later and prunes into adolescence.

test.q: Which protein pair links the presynaptic and postsynaptic sides of a new synapse?
test.explain: Neurexins bind neuroligins to organize synapses. The other pairs are axon guidance cues.

test.q: During pruning, which cells engulf complement-tagged synapses?
test.explain: Microglia use the complement receptor CR3 to engulf synapses tagged with C1q and C3.

test.q: A 'silent' synapse in the developing cortex has:
choices: NMDA receptors but no AMPA receptors
Gap junctions but no chemical receptors
AMPA receptors but no NMDA receptors
GABA receptors but no glutamate receptors
test.explain: Silent synapses have NMDA receptors only. Activity inserts AMPA receptors and switches them on.

test.q: What did Hubel and Wiesel show by covering one eye in kittens?
choices: Cortical input from the covered eye shrank
The covered eye grew extra retinal neurons
Both eyes lost their visual cortex input
Myelination of the optic nerve was blocked
test.explain: During a critical period, the deprived eye loses cortical territory and the open eye takes over.

test.q: What is the general order of myelination?
choices: Caudal to rostral, sensory before association
test.explain: Flechsig's order runs caudal to rostral and central to peripheral, with sensory, then motor, then association areas.

test.q: Why is GABA depolarizing in immature neurons?
test.explain: High NKCC1 and low KCC2 keep internal chloride high, so opening GABA-A channels lets chloride flow out and depolarizes the cell.

test.q: Variants that raise expression of which gene are linked to schizophrenia risk through pruning?
test.explain: Sekar et al. (2016) linked higher C4A expression to schizophrenia, possibly through excessive pruning.

test.q: Myelin allows fast ___ conduction, where signals jump between nodes of Ranvier.
test.explain: Saltatory conduction means the action potential jumps from node to node.

test.q: What is the term for removing weak or unused synapses during development?
test.explain: Pruning refines circuits on a 'use it or lose it' basis.

test.q: A time window when experience strongly shapes circuits is called a critical ___.
test.explain: Critical periods open early in life and close as inhibitory circuits and perineuronal nets mature.

kidTest.q: What is a synapse?
choices: A tiny cell that carries oxygen
A small bone inside your skull
A spot where brain cells meet
kidTest.explain: Synapses are where brain cells pass messages to each other.

kidTest.q: What does pruning do in the brain?
choices: Removes roads that are not used
Adds new bones to the head
kidTest.explain: Like trimming a bush, pruning removes unused connections.

kidTest.q: What does myelin do?
kidTest.explain: Myelin wraps the brain's wires and speeds up messages.

kidTest.q: Which part of the brain finishes its wrapping last?
kidTest.explain: The front of the brain, used for planning, finishes in your twenties.

kidTest.q: What is the fatty coat around brain wires called? m _ _ _ _ n
kidTest.explain: Myelin works like the plastic coat on a charger cord.

advancedTest.q: Mice lacking C1q or C3 show incomplete eye-specific segregation in the thalamus. The best interpretation is:
choices: Complement mainly drives the switch from GABA excitation to inhibition
Complement is needed for retinal axons to reach their target
Complement tags weaker inputs so they can be removed
advancedTest.explain: Axons still reach the thalamus, but without complement tags microglia fail to remove weaker synapses, so segregation stays incomplete.

advancedTest.q: A 2-year-old has diffusely T2-bright white matter, with an otherwise expected T1 pattern and no signs of white matter loss. What is most likely?
choices: Acute demyelination, as seen in multiple sclerosis
Periventricular leukomalacia caused by preterm injury
Hypomyelination, as seen in PLP1 disorders
Normal terminal zones in the peritrigonal region
advancedTest.explain: By about age 2, T2 should look adult-like. Diffuse persistence suggests hypomyelination, unlike focal terminal zones or the white matter loss of PVL.

advancedTest.q: Knockouts of neurexin or neuroligin cause severe dysfunction but only modest synapse loss. This suggests these molecules mainly:
choices: Set the timing of oligodendrocyte birth
Guide growth cones over long distances
Shape how synapses mature and function
Start the first contact between neurons
advancedTest.explain: Synapses still form without them, so their main role is specifying and maturing synaptic function rather than creating contacts.

advancedTest.q: mGluR5 antagonists worked in fragile X mice but failed in human trials. Which explanation best fits the lesson?
choices: Trials began after key critical windows closed
Fragile X is mainly a white matter disorder
The drugs removed myelin in treated patients
FMRP is not expressed in human neurons
advancedTest.explain: Testing at an age when critical windows may have closed, along with poor outcome measures and species differences, are proposed reasons.
